title: "Frequently asked questions"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(digits = 4)
```

Short answers to questions that come up when building a media mix model or
attributing conversions with mediamix. Each one names the functions and
arguments involved, and their help pages have the detail. The examples use
the package's simulated data, `mm_weekly` and `mm_events`.

```{r}
library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)
data(mm_events)
```

## Carryover

### Should the adstock kernel be normalised?

By default (`normalise = TRUE`) the kernel's weights sum to 1, so a steady
spend of 100 a week adstocks to 100 once the filter has filled, and a
coefficient on the adstocked column reads per unit of spend. With
`normalise = FALSE`, the convention Robyn uses, the same spend accumulates to
100 / (1 - decay), and the coefficient reads per unit of accumulated media.
The two series differ only by a constant factor, so in a least-squares fit
only the coefficient's scale changes. A saturation `half_max` given as an
amount belongs to one convention and is wrong for the other, while one set
relative to the series' own reference level, as `step_saturation()` sets it,
gives the same curve under both. Keep one convention for a project, and
compare coefficients only between models fitted the same way.

```{r}
steady <- rep(100, 100)
c(normalised = tail(adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.8), 1),
  raw = tail(adstock_geometric(steady, decay = 0.8, normalise = FALSE), 1))
```

### Why are the first weeks of an adstocked series low?

Every filter starts from zero unless told otherwise, as if nothing had been
spent before the first row. A slow channel takes weeks to fill: at a decay of
0.85 a steady spend reaches 15% of its level in the first week, and 90% only
after `effective_window(0.85)`, `r effective_window(0.85)` weeks. With spend
from before the series, pass `adstock_state()` of it as `state`; without it,
`adstock_steady_state()` gives the state that steady spend at the series'
early average would have left. `warm_start = TRUE` in the tuners and
`start = "steady"` in `step_adstock()` apply the same correction. Robyn's
remedy, adstocking every row and fitting the model on the later rows only,
works here too.

```{r}
x <- rep(100, 6)
rbind(cold = adstock_geometric(x, decay = 0.85),
      steady = adstock_geometric(x, decay = 0.85,
                                 state = adstock_steady_state(x, decay = 0.85)))
```

### How long should `max_lag` be?

The default, `max_lag = Inf`, runs the geometric kernel as a recursive filter
and never truncates it, so there is nothing to choose. A finite kernel should
keep most of the effect: `effective_window(decay, coverage)` is the smallest
number of periods that holds `coverage` of a geometric kernel's total weight.
The same number checks a fitted decay, since an effective window that
approaches the length of the series is not identified by the data. The
Weibull and delayed kernels have no recursive form and always need a finite
`max_lag`; `effective_window()` of a comparable geometric decay is a starting
point.

```{r}
effective_window(c(tv = 0.85, search = 0.15), coverage = 0.9)
effective_window(0.85, coverage = 0.99)
```

### How do I convert a half-life between daily and weekly data?

`decay_from_half_life()` and `half_life()` take `period`, the spacing between
rows in the unit the half-life is stated in. A 21-day half-life on weekly
data is `decay_from_half_life(21, period = 7)`, the same decay as a three-week
half-life, and `half_life(decay, period = 7)` gives a weekly decay's half-life
in days. To move a decay fitted on daily data to weekly data, go through its
half-life:

```{r}
daily <- 0.9
days <- half_life(daily)
c(days = days, weekly = decay_from_half_life(days, period = 7),
  daily_to_the_7th = daily^7)
```

The half-life is kept and the decay per row changes. Adstocking weekly totals
is still not the same as adstocking daily spend and summing it to weeks,
because the timing of spend within each week is lost.

### How do I choose the decay?

Choose it against the KPI, by cross-validation. `tune_carryover()` scores each
candidate `(max_lag, decay)` for one channel by how well a model fitted on the
adstocked media predicts held-out KPI, on forward-only splits, with trend,
price and seasonality passed as `controls`. `tune_carryover_joint()` does the
same for every channel inside one model, so no channel is credited with
another's effect, and `plot()` on either result shows how sharply the data
identifies each decay. To tune carryover together with saturation and a model
penalty, use `step_adstock_channels()` or `step_adstock()` with
`step_saturation()` and `tune()` in a tidymodels workflow, as
`vignette("tidymodels")` shows; that search needs the tune, parsnip, workflows
and yardstick packages.

### What is the difference between `best` and `best_1se`?

`best` is the candidate with the lowest cross-validated error. `best_1se` is
the shortest carryover (lowest half-life, then shortest kernel) whose error is
within one standard error of `best`'s, the one-standard-error rule of Breiman
et al. (1984) and Hastie et al. (2009), with the standard error taken from the
paired difference between the two over the same splits. Carryover is often
weakly identified, so the two can differ widely, and when they do the data
cannot tell them apart. The shorter one is the more cautious claim about how
long a channel keeps working, though not for every decision, since it also
lowers the channel's marginal return. In `tune_carryover_joint()` the rule is
applied channel by channel, and `best_1se_metric` scores the resulting set as
a whole.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
spend <- pmax(0, rnorm(120, 500, 250))
kpi <- 200 + 0.5 * adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.7) + rnorm(120, sd = 60)
tuned <- tune_carryover(spend, kpi, decays = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1))
rbind(best = tuned$best, one_se = tuned$best_1se)
```

The true decay here is 0.7, and the noise leaves the data unable to separate
`r tuned$best_1se$decay` from `r tuned$best$decay`.

### How do I adstock several geographies?

Pass the geography as `by`. Each group is filtered on its own, so carryover
never runs from the last week of one geography into the first week of the
next, and each group's rows must be in time order, since the transforms have
no time index. `media_transform()`, `transform_plan()`, `marginal_roi()`,
`simulate_plan()` and `allocate_budget()` take `by` too, the tuners take `by`
with `index`, and `step_adstock()` takes `by` and sorts by its own `index`.
Do not rely on `dplyr::group_by()` instead: the grouping does not survive into
every place the transforms run, such as a recipe's `bake()`, and
`diagnose_media()` ignores it with a message naming the `by` to pass.

```{r}
spend <- c(100, 0, 0, 200, 0, 0)
geo <- rep(c("north", "south"), each = 3)
rbind(pooled = adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5),
      by_geo = adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5, by = geo))
```

### What happens when weeks are missing?

The transforms treat adjacent rows as adjacent periods. A missing week lets
the decay act once across what were two weeks, a repeated week is carried
over twice, and a row out of order mixes later spend into earlier weeks, and
none of these raises an error. Given the time column as `date`,
`diagnose_media()` counts each of them per series in its `dates` table and
lists them in `flags`, and `step_adstock()` warns at `prep()` when its index
is unevenly spaced and stops on a repeated time point. Add a row for every
missing period before transforming, with zero spend where the channel did not
run. A missing value in a row that exists is an error in the adstock
functions by default; `na_action = "zero"` reads it as no spend, and
`step_adstock()` does that by default.

```{r}
gappy <- mm_weekly[-10, ]   # drops one week of north
diagnose_media(gappy, media = "tv", by = "geo", date = "date")$dates
```

## Saturation

### Does saturation go before or after adstock?

Saturation goes after adstock. A saturation curve caps what the media
pressure in a period can achieve, and that pressure includes carryover from
earlier weeks. Saturating first puts each week's spend through the curve on
its own, so carryover never counts towards saturation, and with
`normalise = FALSE` the carried-over values can add up past the ceiling.
`media_transform()` adstocks first by default and warns when asked for
`order = "saturate_then_adstock"`, and in a recipe `step_saturation()` goes
after `step_adstock()`. Robyn uses the same order.

### Why is `half_max` a fraction in `step_saturation()`?

In `saturate_hill()` and `media_transform()`, `half_max` is an amount of
adstocked media, the level at which the response reaches half its ceiling, so
it depends on each channel's scale. `step_saturation()` takes it as a fraction
of each column's reference level in the training data, its largest value by
default (`ref = "max"`), so one tunable value means the same thing for every
channel. A `half_max` of 0.4 there puts the half-way point at 40% of the
largest adstocked value seen in training, and with `by` each geography gets a
reference of its own.

## Reporting

### What does "(baseline)" mean?

`contributions()` gives each channel its coefficient times its transformed
column, period by period, and pools everything else the model predicts into a
channel called `"(baseline)"`: the intercept, trend, price, seasonality,
holidays and any other control. It is the model's prediction minus the media
effect, which is what makes each period's contributions sum to the
prediction. It holds whatever this decomposition does not attribute to media,
and reporting it as organic demand overstates what the model knows. For
periods the model was not fitted on, pass `newdata` so that the baseline
comes from `predict()`; for a bare coefficient vector it is the intercept
alone.

```{r}
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]], shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
media <- transform_plan(north, spec)
media$week <- seq_len(nrow(media))
fit <- lm(revenue ~ tv + video + search + social + display + week + price +
            seasonality + holiday, data = media)

contrib <- contributions(media[channels], fit, index = media$date)
round(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$channel, sum))
```

### Should I use `roi()`, `marginal_roi()` or `mroi()`?

`roi()` is the average return, each channel's total contribution divided by
its total spend, which scores the period as a whole. `marginal_roi()` is the
return on the next unit of spend. It re-runs carryover and saturation on a
budget 1% larger (`lift = 0.01`) and divides the extra response by the extra
spend, following Jin et al. (2017), so it is the one to use when moving
budget.
`mroi()` is the slope of a saturation curve at one level of transformed
media, a property of the curve rather than a return on spend. Under a concave
curve the marginal return is below the average one everywhere; under an
S-shaped curve, below its inflection point, it can be above.

```{r}
marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
```

The `roi` column is the average return that `roi()` reports from these
contributions, and `mroi` the marginal return beside it.

### Why does `marginal_roi()` stop counting at the last week?

By default (`extend = 0`) it sums response over the observed weeks only, the
weeks `contributions()` and `roi()` cover, so that its average return matches
theirs. The carryover of spend near the end of the data then falls outside the
sum, which understates the marginal return of slow channels. For a budget
decision, pass `extend = effective_window(decay, 0.99)`, which appends that
many weeks of zero spend so the late carryover plays out.

```{r}
tv_mroi <- function(extend) {
  marginal_roi(north$tv, coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
               adstock = spec$tv$adstock, saturation = spec$tv$saturation,
               extend = extend)$mroi
}
c(observed_weeks = tv_mroi(0),
  with_run_out = tv_mroi(effective_window(truth$decay[["tv"]], 0.99)))
```

### How do I report by geography or by year?

Give `contributions()` the grouping as `by`, and pass the same grouping to
`roi()`, which then returns one row per channel per group. For one year or
quarter of a longer decomposition, give `roi()` the period of each row of
spend as `index` and the periods to keep as `periods`. `rows` in
`marginal_roi()` raises spend only inside a planning window, and
`simulate_plan()` and `allocate_budget()` take `by` for a panel.

```{r}
year <- format(media$date, "%Y")
by_year <- contributions(media[channels], fit, index = media$date, by = year)
roi(by_year, north[channels], by = year)
```

### Where do intervals come from, and what do they leave out?

`block_bootstrap()` puts percentile intervals on any statistic computed from a
weekly table, such as coefficients, contributions or returns. It resamples
blocks of consecutive weeks, so the autocorrelation that carryover creates
survives (Künsch, 1989), then refits and recomputes through your `statistic`
function. Transform the media first and put the transformed columns in the
data, so that no block carries spend across a join. The intervals cover
sampling variation given the model and its transform parameters; they leave
out the uncertainty in choosing those parameters and any error in the
specification, and on short series they cover less than their nominal level,
so read them as a lower bound. Make blocks at least as long as the longest
channel's `effective_window()`, and for a panel pass `by`, so that every
geography takes the same blocks of weeks.

## Budgets

### How do I compare plans or split a budget?

`simulate_plan()` runs each channel of a spend plan through its transform and
coefficient, and with `baseline` it reports each channel's change against
another plan. `reallocate()` builds such a plan by moving an amount from one
channel to another, and `allocate_budget()` splits a total across channels to
maximise the predicted response within `lower` and `upper` bounds, searching
a grid of `steps` increments so that S-shaped curves do not trap it. Both
keep each channel's weekly pattern and change only its level, so neither can
start a channel that has no spend until it is given small weights in the
weeks it should run; to try a different timing, build the plan yourself and
pass it to `simulate_plan()`. The answers are only as good as the fitted
curves, which are identified only over the spend levels in the data, so a
move far beyond them is extrapolation and worth testing before it is made.

```{r}
allocate_budget(north, spec, coef(fit), steps = 100)
```

## Attribution

### Why do the attribution rules disagree?

Each rule is a convention for dividing a conversion among the touches before
it, and the conventions favour different positions: first-touch credits the
channels that open journeys and last-touch those that close them.
`attribute()` runs all six rules on the same journeys, `attribution_spread()`
reports each channel's lowest and highest share, and `channel_positions()`
shows which channels open or close journeys. A wide spread is itself the
finding, since it measures how much of a channel's credit comes from the
choice of rule rather than from the data.

```{r}
paths <- build_paths(mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
                     timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion")
spread <- attribution_spread(attribute(paths))
spread[, c("channel", "min_share", "max_share", "first_last_ratio")]
```

### Can I attribute by segment, with intervals?

Yes. Carry the segment column into the journeys with the `keep` argument of
`build_paths()`, give each journey a single value, and pass the column to
`attribute()` as `by`; every rule, the Markov chain included, then runs on
each segment's journeys alone. With `times` (and `seed`), `attribute()` adds
percentile intervals by resampling journeys with replacement. The intervals
show how far the shares move with the sample of journeys, with the journey
construction and each rule held fixed; they say nothing about the choice of
rule, which `attribution_spread()` measures.

### Can I fit higher-order Markov chains?

`markov_removal()` fits the first-order chain, following Anderl et al.
(2016). For higher orders, export the journeys with `as_channel_paths()` and
pass them to `ChannelAttribution::markov_model()` with its `order` argument
and the same `sep` on both sides; `ChannelAttribution::choose_order()`
suggests an order. That needs the ChannelAttribution package, which mediamix
suggests but does not require. For order 1 the two packages implement the
same removal-effect definition, ChannelAttribution by simulation.

```{r eval = FALSE}
ca <- as_channel_paths(paths, sep = ">")
ChannelAttribution::markov_model(ca, var_path = "path",
                                 var_conv = "total_conversions",
                                 var_null = "total_null", order = 2, sep = ">")
```

### Why keep the journeys that did not convert?

Markov removal effects compare the chance of reaching a conversion with the
chance of reaching nothing, and the journeys that ended in nothing are the
only evidence of the second. Without them the baseline conversion probability
is 1, and every removal effect moves, up or down depending on how the dropped
journeys differed from the converting ones. `build_paths()` keeps them by
default (`keep_null_paths = TRUE`), `as_channel_paths()` counts them in
`total_null`, and `markov_removal()` warns when a table has none.

### How do I choose a lookback window?

Read it off your own journeys. `conversion_lag()` reports quantiles of the
time from first touch to conversion, so a lookback at its 90% point leaves
nine in ten converting journeys whole. Run it on journeys built without
`lookback`, since a lookback caps every lag it measures, and read the lags in
the journey table's `units`, days by default.

```{r}
conversion_lag(paths)
```

## Other tools

### Can I use the transforms with brms, Stan or glmnet?

Yes, with the transform parameters fixed before the fit. The transforms are R
functions on numeric vectors, so `media_transform()` or `transform_plan()`
produces columns that any model can take. `contributions()` reads
coefficients through `coef()`, which serves `lm()`, `glm()` and the fixed
effects of nlme and lme4; for glmnet, brms or Stan, pass the point estimates
as a named vector, naming the intercept `"(Intercept)"` or giving it as
`intercept`, and the baseline is then that intercept alone. `marginal_roi()`,
`simulate_plan()` and `allocate_budget()` take coefficients as a named vector
in any case. To estimate a decay or a `half_max` inside a Bayesian model, the
transform has to be written in that model's own language, Stan for brms.

```{r eval = requireNamespace("glmnet", quietly = TRUE)}
# A ridge regression at a fixed penalty, chosen for illustration
X <- as.matrix(media[c(channels, "week", "price", "seasonality", "holiday")])
ridge <- glmnet::glmnet(X, media$revenue, alpha = 0, lambda = 50)
b <- as.matrix(coef(ridge))[, 1]
marginal_roi(north, b, spec = spec)
```

### Can I reproduce Robyn's transforms?

Yes, for geometric and Weibull CDF adstock with Hill saturation. Given the
series Robyn transformed and its modelling window, `from_robyn()` converts one
channel's `theta` (or `shape` and `scale`), `alpha` and `gamma` into the
`adstock` and `saturation` lists that `media_transform()` takes, and the
result matches Robyn's series. Set `inflexion = "range"` for a model fitted by
Robyn 3.7.0 to 3.11.1, which placed the Hill inflexion point differently.
Robyn's Weibull PDF has no exact equivalent and is refused.
[Migrating from Robyn](migrating-from-robyn.html) works through an example.

### Is any of this causal?

No. A media mix model fitted to observational data is identified only as well
as its specification and the variation in the data allow, and
cross-validation shows predictive value, not a causal mechanism. Attribution
rules, Markov removal effects included, divide observed conversions by a
convention and cannot say what would have happened without a channel.
Randomised experiments, such as geo tests for media and holdouts for digital
channels, measure that, and they are the way to check or calibrate a model;
mediamix has no calibration step of its own. `reallocate()` with `by` sets up
a move in one region, the plan for such a test.
